## The short version

**You do not need to install anything, and you do not need to run any code.**

This session is a guided read-along. {{< var session.presenter >}} writes and runs the
code live on screen. Everything he types is already written out, with its output, in
the [notebook]({{< var site.url >}}notebook.html). Read along in a second window, or
watch and come back to it afterward.

Running the code yourself during the session is **optional**. The setup is below. If
it does not work on the day, follow along.


## What you'll get

| | |
|---|---|
| Notebook (read-along, all outputs shown) | [Linking NaNDA With Your Data: notebook]({{< var site.url >}}notebook.html) |
| Everything as a single download | [Workshop materials (ZIP)]({{< var site.zip >}}) |
| Source and version history | [GitHub repository]({{< var site.repo >}}) |
| Archived and citable | [DOI {{< var site.doi >}}]({{< var site.doi_url >}}) |

The ZIP contains:

- the synthetic dataset and its codebook
- the crosswalk file, the lookup table that turns ZIP codes into Census ZCTAs
- the notebook source, with its Stata and Python equivalents
- an offline copy of this site

**The NaNDA files themselves are not in the ZIP.** NaNDA is distributed through
[ICPSR]({{< var nanda.icpsr_url >}}), which asks for a free account, so you download
your own. It takes about five minutes. The steps are in the optional setup below and
in `data/nanda/README.md` inside the ZIP. You only need them to run the code.

## If you do want to run along

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Optional setup (about 10 minutes, do it before the day)

1. **R** (4.3 or newer): [cran.r-project.org](https://cran.r-project.org/)
2. **RStudio Desktop** (free): [posit.co](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/)
3. Open RStudio and run:

   ```r
   install.packages(c("tidyverse", "here", "janitor"))
   ```

   (`readxl`, which reads the crosswalk, installs as part of `tidyverse`.)

4. Download and unzip the [workshop materials]({{< var site.zip >}}).
5. **Get the NaNDA files from ICPSR.** Sign in at
   [icpsr.umich.edu]({{< var nanda.icpsr_url >}}) with a free account, then download
   these in **R** format (Stata and delimited versions are on the same pages):

   - [**{{< var nanda.social_services_name >}}**]({{< var nanda.social_services_doi >}}):
     the ZCTA 2010 file.
   - [**{{< var nanda.parks_name >}}**]({{< var nanda.parks_doi >}}): dataset 2
     (DS0002), "Parks by ZIP Code Tabulation Area, 2018 (2010 Boundaries)".
   - [**{{< var nanda.ses_name >}}**]({{< var nanda.ses_doi >}}): datasets 3 and 8
     (DS0003 and DS0008).

   Unzip each one, extract the data file from the nested folders, and put all four in
   `data/nanda/` inside the unzipped workshop folder. `data/nanda/README.md` has the
   filenames and the same steps in more detail.

6. Open `workshop.Rproj`, then open `notebook.qmd`, and run the first chunk. If it
   prints a preview of the data, you're set.

**Stata and Python users:** equivalent `.do` files are in the `stata/` folder of the
ZIP and `.py` scripts in `python/`. The live session is in R, but these do the same
thing step for step and are yours to keep. The R code is also there as plain scripts
in `r/`, and each folder carries a second script for data that already has a 2010
tract ID instead of a ZIP code.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## If setup doesn't work

Save the troubleshooting for later. The notebook shows every output. Follow along on
screen, and email us afterward: [{{< var nanda.contact >}}](mailto:{{< var nanda.contact >}}).

## What we assume you already know

You have used R, Stata, or another statistical package to open a dataset and join two
tables. This session covers what goes wrong when you link individual-level data to
neighborhood-level data, and how to catch it, in whichever
language you use.
